title: GitOps Fundamentals
summary: Pull-based, git-as-source-of-truth deployment, and how a reconciling agent replaces a pipeline that pushes changes out.

slides.markdown:
Every deploy mechanism differs on **who initiates the change**.

| Model | Who initiates | Credentials needed |
|---|---|---|
| Push-based CD | The CI pipeline runs `kubectl apply`/`helm upgrade` against the cluster | The pipeline needs cluster-write credentials |
| Pull-based GitOps | An agent *inside* the cluster watches a git repo and applies changes itself | The cluster needs read-only git credentials; nothing external needs cluster-write access |

**How to decide:** pull-based GitOps is the stronger default for anything security-sensitive, since it eliminates external systems holding cluster-admin credentials at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Git as the single source of truth
slides.markdown:
In GitOps, the cluster's **desired state** — every Deployment, Service, ConfigMap — is defined declaratively in a git repository, not in whatever someone last `kubectl apply`'d by hand. The repo isn't documentation of the cluster; it *is* the specification the cluster is supposed to match.

This gives infra changes the same guarantees app code changes get: PR review, a commit history that's an audit trail, and `git revert` as a rollback mechanism.

A GitOps agent (Argo CD, Flux) runs a continuous loop: pull desired state from git, observe the cluster's actual state, diff the two, and apply whatever converges them — then repeat.

![The GitOps reconciliation loop](assets/reconciliation-loop.svg)

This is the same reconcile pattern every Kubernetes controller uses, just aimed at "does the cluster match git" instead of "does this resource match its spec."

Because the agent's loop runs continuously, it doesn't just deploy — it **watches for drift**. If someone manually `kubectl edit`s a Deployment in a moment of panic, the next reconciliation cycle sees the cluster no longer matches git and reverts the manual change back to what's declared.

This is a feature, not a bug: it makes git the *only* durable way to change the cluster, which is exactly the guarantee GitOps is selling. Manual changes become temporary at best.

slides.sectionTitle: A merged PR, no separate deploy step
slides.markdown:
Trace the full flow: an engineer merges a PR that bumps an image tag in a manifest repo. The GitOps agent's next poll (or a git webhook) notices the repo changed, diffs it against the cluster, and applies the new image tag — no one runs a separate `deploy` command, no pipeline stage pushes anything to the cluster.

The merge *is* the deploy trigger. This collapses "merge to main" and "ship to prod" into the same event, which is exactly the point.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: giving the pipeline cluster-admin creds anyway
slides.markdown:
A common half-migration: a team adopts a GitOps *tool* but still has their CI pipeline hold cluster-admin credentials and run `kubectl apply` directly — completely undermining the security benefit. Now there are two ways to change the cluster (git, and the pipeline's standing credentials), and an attacker who compromises the pipeline still gets full cluster access.

Real GitOps means the credentials flow **one direction only**: the in-cluster agent pulls from git using read-only git credentials. Nothing external ever holds write access to the cluster.
